title: The Grapes
subtitle: Why champagne rests on three grapes, what each one brings, and the quieter varieties still waiting in the wings.

episodes.title: Three Grapes, and How They Came to Dominate
episodes.hook: Champagne is often described as a wine of three grapes, and in the glass that is very nearly true. Yet the rules name more than three, and the story of how three came to lead is a story of frost, disease and choice.
cards: The grapes allowed into champagne are listed in the appellation's rulebook, the cahier des charges, which sets out everything a wine must do to carry the name.
For many years that list held seven varieties: Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay, and alongside them Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris.
In 2025 an eighth was added, Chardonnay Rose, a pink-skinned form of Chardonnay, and a disease-resistant newcomer called Voltis has been admitted on trial.
Even so, almost every vine you would see on a walk through the region belongs to one of the three familiar names, and that has been true for generations.
For the 2023 vineyard, the growers' union put Pinot Noir at about 38 per cent, Chardonnay at about 31 per cent and Meunier at about 30 per cent.
Everything else together came to less than one per cent. Other sources round the figures a little differently, and Chardonnay and Meunier often trade places by a point.
So it is fairest to think of the three as close to equal partners, with Pinot Noir a little ahead, rather than to hold on to any single exact figure.
It was not always this way. Before the late nineteenth century, Champagne's vineyards held a much wider and more varied collection of grapes than it does today.
The turning point was phylloxera, a tiny aphid-like insect from America that feeds on vine roots. It was first noticed in Champagne in August 1890, at Tréloup in the Aisne.
The cure, used across Europe, was grafting: European vines were joined onto American rootstocks that could tolerate the insect, and whole vineyards were replanted that way.
Replanting was costly and slow, and when growers had to choose what to put back, they tended to favour reliable, productive varieties over the more awkward old ones.
Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay were the winners of that choice. The older grapes survived only in scattered corners, mostly in the south of the region.
Another change came with the Aube. When its villages were admitted to the appellation in 1927, many had to replace their Gamay with the classic Champagne varieties.
Within the three, the balance kept moving. Several accounts suggest Meunier covered around half of the vineyard in the middle of the twentieth century.
In the decades that followed, Chardonnay is said to have been planted more widely, helped by a growing taste for blanc de blancs, a champagne made only from white grapes.
One French guide describes the proportions as fairly stable since the 1980s, with Chardonnay edging up and Meunier easing back a little.
Each of the three found the parts of the region that suit it best, which is why the map of grapes in Champagne follows its hills, valleys and soils so closely.
That geography is the thread we will follow, one grape at a time, beginning with the black grape that leads them all.
episodes.setup: Pinot Noir is a black grape, yet most of the champagne it goes into is pale gold. How that happens begins at the press, within hours of the harvest.

episodes.title: Pinot Noir, a Black Grape for Mostly White Wine
episodes.hook: Pinot Noir covers more of Champagne than any other grape, and it is a black grape. It is natural to wonder how so much of it ends up in wine as pale as straw.
episodes.callback: We saw how phylloxera and replanting left three grapes leading the vineyard, with Pinot Noir slightly ahead.
cards: The answer lies in where a grape keeps its colour. In Pinot Noir, as in most black grapes, the pigments sit in the skin, while the pulp and juice are nearly colourless.
Those pigments are called anthocyanins. Red wine is red because its juice is left to soak with the skins, drawing the colour out over days.
Champagne does the opposite. Bunches are pressed whole, immediately after picking and slowly, so the juice runs away from the skins before it can take much colour.
The pressing is measured in a unit called a marc, a load of 4,000 kilos of grapes, from which the rules allow at most 2,550 litres of juice.
The first 2,050 litres are the cuvée, the finest and best-balanced juice. The last 500 litres are the taille, richer in colour and generally less refined.
Done with care, that gentle pressing gives a white base wine from black grapes. Leave the juice with the skins on purpose, and you are on the way to a rosé.
Pinot Noir's first great home is the Montagne de Reims, the wooded hill between Reims and Épernay, where it is the main grape in villages such as Bouzy, Ambonnay and Verzenay.
Verzenay sits on the northern flank of the hill, so this is not simply a story of south-facing slopes. Growers have learned which sites ripen Pinot Noir well.
Along the Marne, the stretch known as the Grande Vallée, around Aÿ, is another Pinot Noir stronghold, in a valley otherwise better known for Meunier.
The second great home is far to the south, in the Côte des Bar in the Aube, not far from Burgundy. Here Pinot Noir is the main grape by a wide margin.
Sources put its share in the Côte des Bar at somewhere above 80 per cent, and in villages such as Les Riceys it is almost the only grape planted.
The soils there are different, too. Instead of chalk, the Côte des Bar sits largely on Kimmeridgian marl, a mix of limestone and clay that it shares with Chablis.
Pinot Noir is not an easy grape to grow. It buds early in spring, which leaves its tender new shoots exposed to frost, a risk that remains real in Champagne.
It also has thin skins and tight bunches, so damp weather near harvest can encourage rot, and in this cool, rainy region growers have to watch it closely.
That is why it tends to be given the warmer, well-drained sites, where it can ripen fully before autumn and still hold the freshness that champagne needs.
In a blend, Pinot Noir is usually spoken of as the grape that gives body and structure, the framework on which the other grapes hang their fruit and finesse.
Many houses describe it that way in their own words, though each uses it differently, and a Côte des Bar Pinot Noir can taste quite unlike one from the Montagne.
Sometimes it is bottled on its own, or with Meunier, as a blanc de noirs, a white champagne made only from black grapes, and then its character is easiest to find.
episodes.setup: From the black grape we turn to the white one, and to a long east-facing slope where Chardonnay has made itself almost the only resident.

episodes.title: Chardonnay and the Côte des Blancs
episodes.hook: South of Épernay, a long slope runs through a string of villages where almost every vine is Chardonnay. Understanding why it settled there tells you a great deal about the grape, and about chalk.
episodes.callback: We followed Pinot Noir from the Montagne de Reims to the Côte des Bar, and watched black grapes give white juice.
cards: The slope is the Côte des Blancs, the hillside of the whites. It runs south from near Épernay through villages such as Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger.
In the Atlas's planting figures, those four villages are recorded as entirely Chardonnay, and their neighbours Chouilly and Oiry come very close behind.
Most of the slope faces east, so the vines catch the morning sun. Writers on the region describe that early sun as a help against frost on the young shoots.
Beneath the vines lies chalk, much of it a type known as belemnite chalk, named for the fossils of small, squid-like creatures that lived in the ancient sea here.
Chalk behaves like a sponge. It drains away heavy rain, yet it holds a great deal of water within the rock, which the roots can draw on in a dry summer.
That balance of good drainage and steady moisture suits a grape that can easily become too ripe and broad on rich soils, and needs to keep its freshness.
Chardonnay is a white grape that grows well in many places, from Burgundy to California, but in Champagne it is especially admired for the tension and precision chalk can give it.
The grape has its own difficulties. Like Pinot Noir, it buds early, and in spring frosts the Côte des Blancs has suffered some of the region's heaviest losses.
In the April frosts of 2021, for example, one large house estimated that its Chardonnay lost a greater share of buds than its Pinot Noir or Meunier.
The Côte des Blancs is not Chardonnay's only home. Vertus, at the southern end of the slope, is recorded as mostly Chardonnay with a little Pinot Noir.
Further south, the Côte de Sézanne grows a good deal of Chardonnay, and in the Aube a single chalky hill near Troyes, Montgueux, is known for it too.
Chardonnay also appears all over the rest of the region, in the Montagne and the valley, because almost every blend wants at least a little of it.
When a champagne is made only from white grapes, it may be called a blanc de blancs, and in practice that usually means a wine made entirely from Chardonnay.
Côte des Blancs Chardonnay is the classic source for these wines, and many of them name their village, or even several villages blended along the slope.
Young blanc de blancs is often described as citrus-scented, lean and taut, and with time it can soften into flavours that tasters liken to toast, nuts and cream.
Many writers believe Chardonnay is the grape that ages most gracefully in champagne. It is a widely held opinion, though Pinot Noir and Meunier both have their defenders.
Because the rank of grand cru belongs to whole villages, six of Champagne's seventeen grand cru villages lie here, all of them Chardonnay villages.
episodes.setup: The third grape has spent much of its life in the shadow of the other two. Its home is the valley, and its story begins with a frost-prone river.

episodes.title: Meunier, Long Underrated
episodes.hook: For much of the last century, Meunier was the grape that filled out a blend while its partners took the credit. Its home in the Marne valley explains why it was planted, and why opinions are changing.
episodes.callback: We stood on the chalk of the Côte des Blancs and saw why Chardonnay is almost alone there.
cards: Meunier is named after the miller. The undersides of its leaves are covered in fine white down, so the vine looks as if it has been lightly dusted with flour.
It is a close relative of Pinot Noir and was long known as Pinot Meunier. Champagne now generally calls it simply Meunier, a name the region's own bodies have encouraged.
Its heartland is the Vallée de la Marne, the river valley running west from Épernay, where in many villages it is by far the most planted grape.
Festigny, on the valley's left bank, is recorded in the Atlas's figures as more than four-fifths Meunier, and the left bank as a whole is Meunier's strongest ground.
The valley is a natural place for frost. Cold air sinks and gathers along the lower ground on still spring nights, just when the vines are pushing out their first shoots.
Meunier buds later than Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, so its young shoots often appear after the worst danger has passed. That single habit has made it valuable in frost-prone sites.
It also ripens relatively early, which is a comfort in a cool, damp region, because the grapes can be gathered before autumn weather turns against them.
The valley's soils are generally heavier, with more clay than the Côte des Blancs, and Meunier copes with them well where the other two grapes can struggle.
In the glass, Meunier is usually described as fruity, round and generous, which is exactly why blenders have valued it, especially in non-vintage champagnes.
That usefulness came with a quieter reputation. Meunier was long spoken of as a workhorse, a supporting grape rather than one deserving a bottle of its own.
It was also widely said that Meunier did not age as well as Pinot Noir or Chardonnay. That has always been an opinion, and some notable wines have argued against it.
Krug, among the most celebrated houses, has long included a significant share of Meunier in its blends, which are known for ageing very well.
Among growers, a number have bottled Meunier on its own. Champagne José Michel is one well-known name, and so is La Closerie, Jérôme Prévost's domaine in Gueux.
Since then, more single-variety Meunier champagnes have appeared, often from growers in the valley who know its best slopes and want to show what they can do.
Tasted on its own, good Meunier can be quite a revelation: warm-fruited and supple, yet still fresh, with a character that is unmistakably its own.
None of this means Meunier has replaced the other two. It means that its place in a blend is now more often a choice than a convenience, which is a fine thing.
As springs grow milder and harvests come earlier, Meunier's late budding and early ripening are being looked at again, which adds a new chapter to an old story.
episodes.setup: Behind the three, a handful of older grapes have survived in small corners. Each has a history, and a few growers devoted to keeping them alive.

episodes.title: The Other Four, and the Growers Who Keep Them
episodes.hook: Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris have been part of Champagne for centuries, and they are still allowed today. They are simply very rare, and each rarity has a reason.
episodes.callback: We followed Meunier from the frost-prone valley floor to the growers who bottle it alone.
cards: These four are sometimes called the forgotten varieties, or heritage varieties. They are full members of the rulebook, permitted in the same way as the three leading grapes.
Together they cover a tiny part of the vineyard. Most sources place them, with the other minor grapes, at well under one per cent, though their exact figures differ.
Pinot Blanc is the largest of the four in most accounts. It is a white member of the Pinot family, and in Champagne it is found especially in the Aube.
Pinot Gris is the Pinot family's grey-pink-skinned member, and Champagne growers have traditionally also called it Fromenteau, an old name some producers still use when describing their wines.
Petit Meslier is a white grape, believed from DNA studies to be a cross of two old varieties, Gouais Blanc and Savagnin, and it is known for its very high acidity.
Arbane is the rarest of the four, a white grape with a long history in the southern part of Champagne, especially around Bar-sur-Aube.
Estimates of how much Arbane is left vary widely, from under a hectare to more than ten, so it is safest to say only that very little remains.
Why did they fade? After phylloxera, growers replanting expensive grafted vines tended to choose varieties that produced reliably, and these older grapes often did not.
Petit Meslier, for instance, buds early and is prone to poor fruit set, and Arbane struggles to ripen fully in cool years and suffers in frost and disease.
Their survival owes a great deal to a small number of producers, many of them in the Aube, who have kept old vines or planted new ones on purpose.
Moutard, in the Côte des Bar, bottles a pure Arbane, and a blend called Cuvée Six Cépages that uses six of the seven long-standing varieties.
Drappier, also in the Côte des Bar, makes Quattuor, a blanc de blancs from four white grapes: Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Chardonnay.
Further north, Aubry, which grows all seven, and Tarlant in the Marne valley have both made cuvées built around these grapes, and Laherte Frères near Épernay has one called Les 7.
Les 7 is a reminder that all seven of the long-standing varieties can be blended into one wine, a small, living picture of what Champagne once looked like.
Most of these wines are made in small quantities and are not always easy to find, but they are worth ordering when you see them, for the history as much as the taste.
The newest name in the rulebook comes from the same instinct. Chardonnay Rose, a natural mutation of Chardonnay with pinkish skins, was added in 2025.
It had been registered in the French catalogue of vine varieties in 2018, and the first plantings with certified vines are expected in 2027.
So the list of Champagne grapes is not fixed. It has narrowed over a century, and in the last few years it has quietly begun to widen again.
episodes.setup: One newcomer was admitted not because it was old, but because it resists disease. Its arrival is part of a much larger conversation about the future.

episodes.title: Voltis and a Warming Future
episodes.hook: Voltis is reported to be the first disease-resistant variety admitted to any French appellation, and it is champagne's newest grape. It is still on trial, and its story says a great deal about the pressures the region faces.
episodes.callback: We met the older grapes, and the growers keeping them, and saw Chardonnay Rose added in 2025.
cards: Champagne is cool and often damp, which suits the slow ripening sparkling wine needs, but also suits the fungal diseases that attack vines.
The two most troublesome are downy mildew and powdery mildew. Both can ruin a crop, and controlling them has traditionally meant spraying the vines many times a season.
There is growing pressure, from growers and from the wider public, to use fewer of those treatments, for the soil, for vineyard workers and for the villages among the vines.
One answer is to plant varieties that resist the diseases themselves. In Germany these are often called PIWI grapes, from a German phrase for fungus-resistant vines.
Voltis is one of them. It is a white grape bred jointly by France's agricultural research institute, INRAE, and Germany's Julius Kühn Institute, in a programme begun in 2000.
It was bred to be fully resistant to powdery mildew and highly resistant to downy mildew, so it can be grown with far fewer treatments than the classic varieties.
Its ancestry includes American wild vine species as well as the European wine vine, which is why some people describe it as a hybrid.
Champagne's growers proposed admitting it in 2021, and France's appellation authority, INAO, approved it in early 2022. The amended rules were published at the end of 2022.
It was admitted under a special status, as a variety of interest for adaptation, which allows a carefully limited trial within the appellation.
The limits are firm. A grower may plant Voltis on no more than 5 per cent of their holding, and it may make up no more than 10 per cent of any blend.
Voltis must be blended with other grapes, and the Comité Champagne's guidance says the variety's name may not appear on the label.
The first vines went into the ground in 2023, and the first real harvest of Voltis grapes was gathered in 2025. Only a small area has been planted so far.
The trial runs for a set period, and a decision on whether Voltis stays, leaves or is studied for longer is expected in the early 2030s. Sources differ on the exact year.
Behind the trial sits a second pressure, climate. Champagne's harvests now begin, on average, about twenty days earlier than they did thirty years ago, according to the Comité.
The 2026 harvest was reported as a record early one, with picking allowed from 12 August in the earliest villages.
Warmer seasons bring riper grapes, with more sugar and less acidity, and freshness is the very quality champagne depends on.
That is one reason growers are looking again at how each grape behaves, from Meunier's late budding to the bright acidity of Petit Meslier.
Whether Voltis becomes a lasting part of champagne is still an open question, and it may be one of several answers rather than the only one.
episodes.setup: With every grape now in view, one question remains. What do the words on a label tell you about which grapes are in the bottle, and why is blending the rule?

episodes.title: Blanc de Blancs, Blanc de Noirs, and the Blend
episodes.hook: Some champagne labels tell you exactly which kind of grape went into the bottle, and most say nothing at all. Both are perfectly honest, and the reason lies in the art of blending.
episodes.callback: We followed Voltis through its trial and saw how warmer seasons are reshaping the questions growers ask.
cards: Blanc de blancs means white from whites. It is a champagne made only from white grapes, and in practice that nearly always means Chardonnay alone.
The other white varieties may be used too, which is why Drappier's Quattuor, made from four white grapes, is a blanc de blancs even though it is not all Chardonnay.
Blanc de noirs means white from blacks. It is a champagne made only from black grapes, Pinot Noir, Meunier or both, pressed gently so the wine stays pale.
A blanc de noirs may sometimes show a faint golden or coppery depth, a quiet trace of the skins, and it is often described as fuller and rounder in the mouth.
Both phrases are optional. The Comité Champagne lists them as style descriptions a producer may use, so a wine that fits one of them may still leave it off the label.
Most champagne carries neither phrase, because most champagne is a blend of black and white grapes, and the Comité describes champagne as a great blended wine.
Blending is called assemblage. The winemaker tastes many separate base wines, from different grapes, villages and years, and combines them into a single cuvée.
Each grape brings something. Pinot Noir is usually described as giving body, Chardonnay freshness and finesse, and Meunier fruit and roundness, though every house balances them its own way.
Blending across villages matters as much. A house may join Pinot Noir from the Montagne with Chardonnay from the Côte des Blancs and Meunier from the valley.
Blending across years is the third dimension. Wine kept back from earlier harvests, called reserve wine, lets a house soften a difficult year with the strengths of a better one.
That is how a non-vintage champagne can taste recognisably the same from one bottling to the next, even though no two harvests are alike.
In a way, the three grapes were chosen for this. They ripen at different times, suit different places and bring different qualities, which makes them natural partners.
If frost strikes the early-budding Chardonnay, the later Meunier may be spared. Blending across grapes is also a way of spreading the risks of a cool, unpredictable region.
Single-grape champagnes have their own appeal, because they let you meet one variety, often from one place, without the others alongside it.
Neither approach is better than the other. A blend shows the winemaker's judgement, while a blanc de blancs or blanc de noirs shows a grape and its ground more directly.
So when a label names no grapes at all, it is not hiding anything. It is very likely telling you, by its silence, that three grapes have been brought together on purpose.
episodes.setup: We have come a long way, from phylloxera to Voltis. In our last episode we gather what has held, what is changing, and what we chose to leave out.

episodes.title: Scorecard
episodes.hook: Every thread here ends with an honest account. This is where we gather what has held up, what has been overtaken by events, and what we chose to leave out, with our reasons, so that you can trust the rest.
episodes.callback: We read blanc de blancs and blanc de noirs on the label, and saw why most champagne is a blend.
cards: First, what has held. Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier still make up almost the whole vineyard, with Pinot Noir a little ahead of the other two.
Each grape still follows its ground: Pinot Noir on the Montagne and in the Côte des Bar, Chardonnay on the Côte des Blancs, Meunier in the Marne valley.
Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris remain fully permitted, and a small band of producers continues to grow and bottle them.
Next, what has been overtaken. The familiar phrase that champagne has seven grapes is now out of date, because Chardonnay Rose joined the rules in 2025.
Voltis has moved from proposal to vineyard. It was admitted in 2022, first planted in 2023 and first harvested in 2025, and its trial continues.
And the vineyard's balance is not frozen. Meunier is said to have once covered much more of it, and growers are now looking again at every grape as the climate warms.
Some popular versions deserve a gentle correction. It is easy to see why champagne is called a three-grape wine, but the rules have always named more than three.
Pinot Gris is not a grape lost to Champagne. It still grows here, and its old local name, Fromenteau, is still used by some producers.
Blanc de blancs does not always mean Chardonnay alone. It means white grapes only, and the older white varieties are allowed to join in.
And the idea that Meunier cannot age is best held as an opinion, one that Krug's blends and a number of growers' wines have long gently questioned.
Finally, what we left out, and why. We did not give hectare figures for each of the older grapes, because the sources we found disagreed far too widely.
We gave the grape shares for 2023 as the growers' union published them. Other sources differ by a point or so, often swapping Chardonnay and Meunier.
We did not give a precise share for Meunier in the 1950s or for Chardonnay at any earlier date, because we found no official historical series to rely on.
We left out the exact length of the Voltis trial and the area planted so far, because sources give different periods and figures.
We did not date the final disappearance of Gamay from the Aube, because the accounts we found point to several different years.
We have not named a single grape as the one that ages longest. That question belongs to tasters and to your own cellar, and opinions differ.
Nor have we described the parentage of Arbane or the full ancestry of Voltis, because we could not confirm them from sources we trusted.
Thank you for reading this far. We hope the next time you raise a glass, you can picture the hillsides and valleys where its grapes were grown.
